title: Types and values
Types and values
Reading and writing
text:
read_* functions return a DataFrame. scan_* functions return a LazyFrame, so filters and column selections are pushed into the reader. DataFrame::write*() writes a file; LazyFrame::sink*() streams a query’s result to a file without collecting it in memory.
Parquet, IPC, and JSON support are Cargo features. An extension built without one raises a ComputeError from that format’s functions.

title: DataFrame and LazyFrame
text: DataFrame holds data in memory and runs each operation immediately. LazyFrame records operations and runs them, optimized, on collect(). Both have the same verbs; a DataFrame builds each verb on a lazy query and collects it, as py-polars does.

title: DataFrame and LazyFrame
DataFrame and LazyFrame
text:
Joins
join() takes on, or leftOn and rightOn, and how: inner, left, right, full, semi, anti, or cross. suffix names clashing right-hand columns, coalesce merges key columns, nullsEqual lets null keys match, and maintainOrder (none, left, right, left_right, right_left) fixes the row order.
$sales = read_csv('sales.csv')->select('id', 'store', 'units')->head(6);
$stores = read_csv('stores.csv')->filter(col('store')->ne('S2'));

echo $sales->join($stores, on: 'store', how: 'left', maintainOrder: 'left'), "\n";
echo $sales->join($stores, on: 'store', how: 'anti'), "\n";
echo $stores->rename(['store' => 'shop'])->join($sales, leftOn: 'shop', rightOn: 'store', how: 'inner')->height(), " matched rows\n";

phplyr pipelines on three backends

The results of all backends are compared.

title: Performance
text:
Where the time goes
Polars runs the verbs themselves 10 to 100 times faster than the in-memory frame. Returning rows to PHP is the cost that remains. Collecting 1M rows into PHP takes about 0.2 s for plain columns, plus about 0.5 s per datetime column, because each DateTimeImmutable is a PHP object.
PolarsTable is the faster backend when a pipeline reduces the data (summaries, filters, joins followed by summaries) or chains several verbs before collecting. Reading files with Phpolars\read_csv() or read_parquet() and wrapping the result with PolarsTable::fromPolars() also avoids parsing the file in PHP.
A verb given a PHP closure converts the table to a phibble Frame and back, about 1 s per million rows with a datetime column. On large data, use expressions, or use the in-memory Frame for closure-heavy pipelines.

The optional features cost little: all of them together add about 5 MB. Most of the size is the Polars query engine, expression set, and data types that the core API needs. The dist profile uses opt-level = "s", which is 30% smaller than opt-level = 3 and as fast on the benchmark above (the read_csv → filter → groupBy pipeline on 1M rows). opt-level = "z" halves the size again but doubles single-threaded time. A clean dist build takes 4–5 minutes on an Apple M5 Ultra.

title: Getting started
text:
phpolars needs PHP 8.5 (non-thread-safe), Linux or macOS, a stable Rust toolchain, and libclang. Install it with PIE:
pie install erikwestlund/phpolars
PIE runs Cargo, so the first install takes several minutes. Prebuilt Linux binaries are attached to releases; see Deployment.
From a checkout:
PHP=$(which php) PHP_CONFIG=$(which php-config) cargo build --profile dist
php -d extension=$PWD/target/dist/libphp_polars.so script.php   # .dylib on macOS
On macOS with Homebrew, also set LIBCLANG_PATH=$(brew --prefix llvm)/lib. When several PHP versions are installed, point PHP and PHP_CONFIG at PHP 8.5, because the build uses that PHP’s headers.

title: Getting started
text:
Lazy queries
A LazyFrame records operations and optimizes them before running. scan_csv() starts one from a file, and collect() runs it:
$query = scan_csv('sales.csv')
    ->filter(col('units')->gt(5))
    ->groupBy('store')
    ->agg(col('units')->sum())
    ->sort('store');

echo $query->explain(), "\n\n";
echo $query->collect();

  AGGREGATE[maintain_order: false]
    [col("units").sum()] BY [col("store")]
    FROM
    Csv SCAN [sales.csv]
    PROJECT 2/6 COLUMNS
    SELECTION: col("units") > 5
    ESTIMATED ROWS: 201

title: Deployment
text:
pie install erikwestlund/phpolars
PIE builds the extension with Cargo’s dist profile (fat LTO, opt-level = "s", stripped) and enables it. A build needs a stable Rust toolchain and libclang, and takes several minutes. The extension supports PHP 8.5, non-thread-safe builds, on Linux and macOS.

title: Deployment
text:
Prebuilt binaries
The packaging workflow builds the extension inside the official php:8.5-fpm-bookworm image, installs it with PIE, runs the release checks, and sends real requests through PHP-FPM. It then packages the tested php_polars.so for amd64 and arm64 with:

manifest.json: PHP version and API number, architecture, glibc, the Rust version, the Cargo.lock hash, and the extension’s SHA-256.
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt: the licenses of every Rust dependency compiled into the binary.
INSTALL.txt: copy the file to php-config --extension-dir, add extension=php_polars.so, and set php_polars.max_threads.

Release builds attach these archives to the GitHub release. They target Debian Bookworm’s glibc and are not portable to Alpine (musl). Other platforms build from source with PIE.

title: Deployment
text:
Threads under PHP-FPM
Polars runs queries on a thread pool. FPM workers are separate processes, so each worker that uses phpolars starts its own pool. The INI setting caps the pool per process:
; php.ini
extension=php_polars.so
php_polars.max_threads = 2
The setting defaults to 2 and is PHP_INI_SYSTEM, because the pool starts once per process and cannot be resized. An explicit POLARS_MAX_THREADS environment variable takes precedence. Phpolars\thread_pool_size() reports the size in effect. Size it so that pm.max_children × max_threads fits the machine’s cores.
PHP closures never run on Polars threads. Every phpolars operation is built from expressions that Polars evaluates natively.

title: Deployment
text:
Memory
Polars allocates with its own allocator, outside PHP’s memory manager, so its memory does not count against memory_limit. Reading a 1M-row CSV raises a process’s resident memory to about 83 MB while memory_get_peak_usage() reports 2 MB. Size FPM pools by process memory, and limit request data with the application’s own checks.

title: Deployment
text:
Checking an installation
tests/deployment.php runs the same assertions through the CLI and, in scripts/check-fpm and scripts/check-container, through a real FastCGI request:
php tests/deployment.php
docker build --target checks -f docker/Dockerfile -t php-polars-checks .
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile -t php-polars-runtime .
scripts/check-container php-polars-runtime php-polars-checks

title: Coming from py-polars

title: phpolars
text: phpolars brings Polars to PHP as a native extension written in Rust. It follows the py-polars API: the same classes, methods, and semantics, with camelCase method names and snake_case functions. A test suite compares 169 cases against py-polars 1.43.2, and all of them match.

title: phpolars
text:
What it includes

DataFrame and LazyFrame with py-polars’ verbs: select, withColumns, filter, sort, groupBy/agg, join, unique, pivot, unpivot, explode, describe, and more.
Expressions with arithmetic, three-valued logic, aggregations, window functions (over), when/then/otherwise, and the str, dt, list, struct, and name namespaces.
Series, with the same expression methods.
CSV, Parquet, JSON, NDJSON, and Arrow IPC reading and writing, with lazy scans and streaming sinks.
A thread-pool cap for PHP-FPM (php_polars.max_threads).
An adapter, Phpolars\Phibble\PolarsTable, that runs phibble and phplyr pipelines in Polars.

title: phpolars
text:
The family
phpolars is one of a set of PHP 8.5 packages for data work. phibble is a pure-PHP data frame and the shared table contract. phplyr adds dplyr verbs on top of it. php-stats fits regression and mixed models. phpolars is the optional fast backend: install it when the data is large or the pipeline is heavy, and keep using phplyr’s verbs.

title: phibble and phplyr
text: The erikwestlund/phpolars-phibble package provides Phpolars\Phibble\PolarsTable, an implementation of phibble’s table contract backed by a Polars DataFrame. phplyr’s verbs work on any table that implements the contract, so a phplyr pipeline runs in Polars when it starts from a PolarsTable.

title: phibble and phplyr
text:
What runs in Polars
Verbs given column names or phibble expressions (Phibble\Expr, which phplyr’s helpers such as col(), mean(), and n() build) run in Polars. The translation follows dplyr’s semantics, the same ones phibble’s in-memory Frame uses:

NA propagates, logic is three-valued, and aggregates default to na_rm = FALSE.
In a grouped mutate() or filter(), aggregates and window functions run per group.
Groups are visited and summarised in sorted key order, with factors in level order and NA last.
Joins follow dplyr 1.2, including join_by() inequality and rolling joins.
round() follows R 4, and quantile() over NA without na_rm raises R’s error.

The adapter’s tests run phibble’s own dplyr reference fixtures (69 expression cases, the contract cases, and 14 join_by() cases) against PolarsTable, and assert that they run without falling back.

title: phibble and phplyr
text:
Closures
PHP closures cannot run on Polars threads. A verb given a closure, such as filter(fn ($r) => $r->units > 0), converts the table to a phibble Frame, runs there, and converts the result back. PolarsTable::$fallbacks counts these conversions. Converting 1M rows costs roughly a second when the table has a datetime column, so pipelines on large data should use expressions. See Performance.

title: Expressions
text:
An Expr describes a computation on columns. Expressions are built with col(), lit(), when(), and the other functions below, and are evaluated by frame verbs such as select(), withColumns(), filter(), and agg(). They never hold PHP closures, so Polars runs them on its own threads.
Operands of comparison and arithmetic methods may be an Expr or a PHP value. PHP strings there are string literals.

title: Expressions
text:
Windows and order
over() evaluates an expression within groups and maps the result back to every row. orderBy sets the order for order-dependent expressions such as cumSum() and shift().
$sales = read_csv('sales.csv', tryParseDates: true)->filter(col('store')->eq('S1'))->head(8);

echo $sales->select(
    'date',
    'product',
    'units',
    col('units')->sum()->over('product')->alias('product_total'),
    col('units')->cumSum()->over('product', orderBy: 'date')->alias('running'),
    col('units')->shift()->over('product', orderBy: 'date')->alias('previous'),
    col('units')->rank('dense', descending: true)->alias('rank'),
);
